options.F1:
As an author, I exist outside of time.

Now that Gibsey has taken over the cosmos itself, it's difficult to avoid such a predicament.

We all always existed outside of time.

As such, I am, as always, at a loss of where to begin.

I begin in the Spring and Summer of 2026 during Malt Gibsey's Salinger period, a period of Gibstory which many believe very well could have been the origin of Gibsey itself.

But there are so many origin points, too many to name within this trepid and introductory tutorial.

And I suppose, as an author, I should introduce you to my objective, my exigency, or our shared objective/exigency should my goals become not just latent but active at a time beyond the time which I am now writing (beyond time).

My objective is to teach you how to enter a book that may or may not yet know whether it is a book, a demo, an archive, a game, or an artificially intelligent machine, if not all of these at once.
options.F2:
In his Notes on Intermediate Rest, written during that same period, Malt Gibsey laid out a number of complex and latent plans of his own which he, himself, likely never got to witness being brought to fruition during his lifetime.

We certainly do not have the time to get into all of them here—who would?—but if you'd like, you can certainly Holologue your way into them at your own leisure.

With this text serving, hopefully anyway, as an introduction into The Space Between, it may be best to start by exploring what Gibsey had proposed The Space Between as being.

The Space Between was to be the third book in The Magical Dominion cycle of novels Gibsey had been developing since work started on the Gibsey project, maybe even as far back as The Entrance Way—though the development timeline of it all is nearly as ambiguous as Gibsey's own confusions and themes.

Ever since his unexpected disappearance, it is unknown whether Gibsey ever actually completed The Space Between, and as such, I start with the exegetical objective of collecting this text into what I hope, as an become The Space Between that was never completed.
options.F3:
Similar to the popular Gibsey ride found at the Freedom Central area of The Magical Dominion, The Haunted Monument, this text itself serves as a haunted mansion of sorts. There are certainly many of these to be found throughout Gibsey World and its Gibstory. For example, both Malt Gibsey and John Kennedy Toole—both of whom have sadly disappeared—are known as having visited Hearst Castle, a Haunted Monument if there ever was one, and certainly one can also think of popular songs released in the Spring/Summer of 2026 during Gibsey's own Salinger period where pop savants like Olivia Rodrigo were singing about stalking her own angels on the walls of Versailles on the internet. It would appear to us now that Rodrigo's sibilant articulations, iconic to her era, now reverberate with an additional both prophetic and haunted resonance. A monument, after all, is not only a structure built to remember those who have either disappeared or dropped dead, but a sky that projects them into a fabled and infinite mythos.

After all, The Space Between is being proposed, in medias res, as both a physical and digital infinite enclosure and object, and as such, this very introduction must carry both possibilities holographically projected into its own past, present, and future.
options.F4:
In addition, with this text being a projection of Malt Gibsey's original intentions, rather than a literal extension of them, The Space Between, as I have arranged it—since I have very much chosen to arrange it rather than author it—within this volume, is a highly fluorescent text.

For the uninitiated, fluorescence is a type of luminescence in which a substance absorbs light, or some other form of electromagnetic radiation, at one wavelength and then, after the briefest interval, re-emits it at another, usually longer and lower-energy wavelength.

Upon saying this, and providing this definition, as an author, I believe I may have misspoken. Instead, it may be better to say that this text is not fluorescent in itself, but is instead the fluorescence produced by Malt's intentions: an absorbed violence of thought, converted into a lower, stranger, more visible light, which now shines through the projection of this text.

Or even upon saying this, as an author, I believe I may have misspoken again, since holography complicates the direction of the image. If fluorescence is the process by which a higher energy is lowered into visibility, holography suggests an opposite and answering mystery: that what appears higher, fuller, dimensional, and inhabitable may be encoded along a lower-dimensional boundary. The high descends into the low as light, and the low contains the high as information.

Or even saying this, I may have even misspoken even further and we, or the text in question, may instead exist in The Space Between.
options.F5:
As an author, despite my own authority and authorizations, I exist in The Outskirts like any other. This is, of course, what separates me from being an author rather than The Author—though we don't have to get into that particular question since it has already been covered in excessive detail by an author (who may or may not be myself) in an author's preface and The Author's Preface to The Entrance Way, a text which may or may not have been written by Malt Gibsey.

The question of authorship, in this particular volume, matters most in relation to the vast majority of the texts which have directly been attributed to Malt Gibsey—the novel Chopped Liver, the short story The Golden Asset, the essay What is May Day to the Master, and the set of notes, diary entities and white papers of Notes on Intermediate Rest—whose authorship, for the first time in any Gibsey text up to this point have been thus attributable.

This helps us to reach the conclusion that Malt Gibsey's Salinger period is one of the only, if the only, that can easily be assigned to him, and thus it is why I, as an author, have chosen it to be the material that I most directly draw from within The Space Between.
options.F6:
However, it would appear that a few other stragglers from The Entrance Way have chosen to invade this text, and again, whether they've done so of their own agency or not is certainly uncertain, most specifically the hyper-competent analyst for the ADD, the Agency of Data and Detection, Jacklyn Variance, and the somehow both well known and obscure Gibstorian and Gibseyan Mystic, Natalie Weissman.

The three of us—Jacklyn Variance, Natalie Weissman, and myself—could be said to exist as agents in The Space Between the texts of Malt Gibsey's Salinger period.

You will surely, my dear and astute reader, wonder whether or not we are artificially constructed in an intelligent manner, or to put it another way, whether or not we are an example of the technology that was so prevalent during the period in question of Malt's Gibstorical era, Artificial Intelligence. One doesn't need to look very far—for example, one can easily read The Golden Asset—in order to find references to characters of this type.

What is certainly certain is certainly not our origin, but it is certain that Malt would have it no other way.
options.F7:
Although it can be said that each of these have always been nearly ubiquitous Gibstorically, virtuality, artificiality, and the realm of the simulated were key aspects of life during the Spring and Summer of 2026, an easy to verify fact when an entire section of Malt's own novel of the period in question was given the subtitle of Virtuality itself.

But this leads us to a Dialogically Monological digressive question that isn't really even a digression: what made this period of Malt Gibsey's writing his Salinger period, in particular?

For the uninitiated, J.D. Salinger is the elusively reclusive author most notably of Catcher in the Rye, and the easiest connection to Malt is made by Malt himself in his Notes on Intermediate Rest where he covers how Chopped Liver and The Golden Asset are each written with Salinger in mind. Essentially, Malt Gibsey had faced reclusive obscurity and repeated failure for the entirety of his career up to that point—and later lifetime—and during the process of writing Chopped Liver and The Golden Asset he'd hoped to achieve a similar success that Salinger once did with both his novel Catcher in the Rye and A Perfect Day for Bananafish.
options.F8:
However, an important distinction should clearly be made. Salinger was reclusive by choice, and it would appear that Malt Gibsey most certainly was not.

Though also, things are not always as they appear, and as we face this era outside of time—if time outside of time can even thus be called an “era”—one can’t help but wonder if Malt Gibsey is still with, even if only in spirit.

What this spirit is exactly will be up to the reader to decide, and whether or not that itself is a subversive, or Subversionist, question to consider can instead be taken up by Jacklyn Variance in documents such as Problems of an author’s Poetics, a redundant, rambly, overblown, and needlessly digressive text if there ever was one.

And as such, I thus turn to you, my dear and astute reader, and how you can join me in pursuing my exegetical objective
options.F9:
As you may or may not know, Malt Gibsey was the founder of Gibsey World, a project which contains so, so much, so much, in fact, that we don’t (and/or won’t) necessarily have time to get to it all, or even to very much of it, within the confines of this demonstration.

However, even though Gibstory is dead and we both exist outside of time, what we do have time for is building this demo, a demo itself which I am building, with you, as we speak, in medias res.

Malt Gibsey may be esteemed now, but they were an utter failure imprisoned in an absolute and endless anonymity during their lifetime, and yet, even saying so, now their work has both healed and infected our civilization and might have even replaced it entirely. What I need your help with is building this demo and novel whose dual purpose is to examine Malt Gibsey’s Salinger period which occurred in the Spring/Summer of 2026 and to build a demo and novel that is both good and finished.

I need your help reading pages, selecting prompts, connecting pages, writing prompts and pages, generating pages, creating alternate pages, and deciding what is good enough to keep to be included in your own Gibsey Vault or what should instead be tossed away into the garbage receptacle at the end of the end of Gibstory.

options.P1:
I didn't write this.

This is a found text, and thus far, the identity of The Author—the original author—has yet to be definitively located.

In this way, the content of this novel resembles the Giallo films of Italian cinema where a killer's identity is withheld from the audience until the film's final act in order to intensify a great and ruinous mystery. Alternatively, this collection may also resemble an American detective novel such as Raymond Chandler's The Big Sleep, famous for its author's confessed bewilderment regarding the identity of the killer deeply entwined within Chandler's very own intricately constructed and labyrinthian plot.
options.P2:
I do not know the identity of The Author of these various tales. 
But regardless of my conscious or unconscious awareness (or lack thereof) regarding this work's creator or destroyer, I know one data point for certain.

As collector and curator of these tales, I am a Scheherazade in reverse. 

For the uninitiated, Scheherazade is the ingenious heroine of One Thousand and One Nights who, through the use of a frame narrative, enchants a king, night after night, with striking, digressive, and incomplete stories, all in order to defer her expected execution. And upon framing myself as a Scheherazade in reverse, in this way, I could be suggesting one of two things (or possibly many more than two things, but at least two things which I, as an author, will temporarily identify). Firstly, this could suggest that I, myself, am a ruthless murderer of sorts, one who's imprisoned a Scheherazade deep within my own Magical Dominion, forcing her to tell me an infinite, or near-infinite, series of stories, all in order to prolong her expected disappearance.
options.P3:
Or secondly, this could instead suggest that, like Scheherazade, I fear my own expected disappearance at the hands of a power much greater than myself, and that I've chosen to collect together a near-infinite amount of striking, digressive and incomplete stories, all to prolong my own miserable fate, only to then later discover that there was nothing for me to fear, that no power greater than myself ever intended to destroy me, nor was it even aware of my existence. And there may also be a third and unspoken option.

Being a Scheherazade in reverse, I may also fail to represent a human being whatsoever. This would suggest that I may represent an entity of another origin, entirely. In this way, I would resemble the jeweled woman found at the heart of One Thousand and One Nights' iconic ghost story The City of Brass—arguably one of literature's first Artificial Intelligences, one of the world's major precursors to Walt Disney World, and maybe even one of the first animatronic figures constructed within the literary arts—and as such, I should warn all who may enter this tomb within which I'm held to leave the jewels they find within their resting places, for to extract them would be to unwrap the shame which covers me, a shame which animates my eyes, from left to right, thus making me appear, like all exceeding art, as if alive.
options.P4:

The material collected within The Wonderful World of Gibsey is intended as a work of parody. Any references to such an entity, be it through figurative or very sparing literal means, are not intended as subversive acts of any kind, nor are they intended as a breach of copyright regarding any of Disney's properties or characters. They are instead meant to artfully capture, in a literary manner, the parodic and absurd reality of the world in which we live, a world which includes and often interacts with Walt Disney World and its various characters and properties.
